usage: Please pass on a message for me.
examples: 부장님께 이 서류 좀 전해 주세요.
Please hand this document to the manager for me.
Tell my friend I said hi.
제 마음을 어떻게 전해야 할지 모르겠어요.
I do not know how to convey how I feel.
nuance: 전하다 is about passing something (a message, regards, an item, a feeling) from one person to another, so the receiver takes 에게/한테 or the honorific 께. 안부를 전하다 ('send one's regards') and 말씀 전해 주세요 ('please pass on the message') are everyday set phrases.
mistakes: Do not confuse 전하다 (pass on / convey) with 전화하다 (make a phone call).

usage: Please let me know the address.
I let them know the result in advance.
examples: Please let me know as soon as you arrive.
If the schedule changes I will let you know in advance.
Do not tell anyone about this yet.
nuance: 알리다 is the causative of 알다 ('to know'), meaning to make someone know something. The most useful everyday form is 알려 주세요 ('please let me know'), which you will say constantly when asking for an address, time, or update.
mistakes: Use 알려 주세요 to ask someone to tell you; plain 알아요 means 'I know' and cannot make a request.

usage: Do not try to talk me into it.
examples: I persuaded the team lead and changed the schedule.
No matter how I try to convince him, my friend will not listen.
I am in the middle of convincing my roommate to come along.
nuance: 설득하다 means to talk someone around to your view through reasoning, and the person you persuade takes 을/를. It is stronger and more deliberate than just 말하다; it implies the other person was reluctant at first.
mistakes: The person persuaded takes 을/를 (사람을 설득하다), not 에게.

usage: It is so hard to say no.
examples: I politely declined the dinner invitation.
It feels awkward to turn down the company dinner.
If it is too much, you can say no.
nuance: 거절하다 is the standard verb for declining a request, offer, or invitation, and the thing refused takes 을/를. For Koreans, directly refusing can feel rude, so it is often softened with 죄송하지만 ('sorry, but') or 정중하게 ('politely').
mistakes: Do not confuse 거절하다 (refuse an offer/request) with 거부하다, which is stronger and feels like a flat rejection.

usage: A parent telling a child off
Please do not scold them too much.
examples: The teacher scolded the students who were being noisy.
I got told off by the team lead for being late.
애를 혼내기 전에 한 번 더 설명해 주세요.
Before you scold the child, please explain one more time.
nuance: 혼내다 means an older or higher-status person verbally disciplining someone beneath them, so the person scolded takes 을/를. The flip side is 혼나다 ('to get scolded'); '나 혼났어' ('I got told off') is something adults still say casually about a boss or partner.
mistakes: Use 혼내다 when you do the scolding and 혼나다 when you are the one being scolded; do not mix them up.

english: to argue a point / call out
usage: I demanded to know why they did it.
examples: 잘못 계산된 것 같아서 가게에 따졌어요.
It seemed miscalculated so I called out the shop.
사소한 거 가지고 너무 따지지 마세요.
Do not split hairs over such small things.
Examine the terms carefully before you sign.
nuance: 따지다 has two flavors: confronting someone to demand an explanation for a wrong, and coolly weighing/scrutinizing details (조건을 따지다, 가격을 따지다). With a person it often sounds combative, so it implies you feel wronged and want answers.
mistakes: With a person, 따지다 sounds confrontational; for a calm question use 물어보다 instead.

usage: Stop being so stubborn about it.
examples: He was clearly wrong but insisted to the end.
친구가 자기가 샀다고 우겨서 그냥 졌어요.
My friend insisted on paying so I just gave in.
Even with proof, he keeps insisting he did not do it.
nuance: 우기다 means to keep insisting you are right even when you are likely wrong, so it carries a clearly negative, stubborn tone. It is everyday spoken Korean among friends and is much more colloquial than the neutral 주장하다 ('to assert').
mistakes: 우기다 implies unreasonable stubbornness; for a neutral, reasoned claim use 주장하다.

usage: The kids are being noisy in the classroom.
Be quiet, do not be so loud.
examples: You must not be noisy in the library.
The next table was so loud it was noisy.
Do not be loud late at night. The neighbors are sleeping.
nuance: 떠들다 is a ㄹ irregular: the ㄹ drops before ㅂ and ㄴ (떠듭니다, 떠드세요) but stays before a vowel (떠들어요). It means making a loud, rowdy racket by talking, and is almost always framed as something you should not do in quiet places.
mistakes: Because it is a ㄹ irregular, the formal form is 떠듭니다, not 떠들습니다.

examples: 그 사람이 가격을 속여서 비싸게 팔았어요.
He lied about the price and sold it expensive.
You must not sign up by lying about your age.
친구를 속이는 건 정말 나쁜 짓이에요.
Deceiving a friend is a really bad thing to do.
nuance: 속이다 is the causative of 속다 ('to be fooled'), meaning to make someone believe something false, so the victim takes 을/를. The passive flip side 속다 / 속았어 ('I got fooled') is just as common in speech.
mistakes: Use 속이다 when you trick someone and 속다 when you are the one fooled (나 속았어 = 'I got tricked').

examples: My friends teased me when they heard my dialect.
You must not make fun of a child's looks.
I teased as a joke but my friend got sulky.
nuance: 놀리다 means making fun of someone, the object taking 을/를, and it ranges from playful ribbing between friends to genuinely hurtful mockery depending on tone. Note this is a different word from the look-alike 놀리다 meaning 'to leave (a hand/machine) idle'.
mistakes: Do not confuse 놀리다 (tease) with 놀다 (play / hang out).

usage: I opened up about my worries.
Feel free to get it all off your chest.
examples: I confided my true feelings to a close friend.
Do not bottle it up alone; open up to someone.
If something is bothering you, you can confide in me anytime.
nuance: 털어놓다 (from 털다 'to shake out' plus 놓다) means to unburden yourself by sharing worries or secrets you have kept inside, and the listener takes 에게/한테. Because the base verb is 놓다, the present contracts to 털어놔요 while the formal stays 털어놓습니다.
mistakes: The 놓- base contracts: it is 털어놨어요 (past), not 털어놓았어요, in normal speech.

usage: I confessed that I like her.
I will be honest and confess.
examples: I worked up the courage and confessed to my crush.
I confessed but got rejected, so I am really upset.
Honestly, I will admit that I lied.
nuance: 고백하다 most often means confessing romantic feelings ('좋아한다고 고백하다'), which for 20-30s is a huge dating-culture moment in Korea, often the official start of a relationship. It also covers admitting a hidden truth or fault, like a heartfelt confession.
mistakes: For romantic confessions use 고백하다; 사과하다 means 'to apologize' and is a different act entirely.
